topics.title: Yield-point phenomenon and strain ageing (Q32–Q38) **[HIGHEST-YIELD TOPIC]**

questions.text: Which statement(s) about *elastic* deformation is/are correct?

statements.text: It is reversible.
Bonds are stretched but no permanent atomic rearrangement occurs.
It obeys Hooke's Law σ = Eε.
Atoms shift by whole lattice vectors and return to equivalent (not original) positions.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 describe elastic deformation. Item 4 describes *plastic* deformation. [P2]
questions.concise: Elastic = reversible, bonds stretched, Hooke's law — whole-lattice-vector shifts belong to *plastic*.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: elastic deformation is reversible.
- Item 2 — TRUE: bonds are stretched but no permanent atomic rearrangement occurs.
- Item 3 — TRUE: it obeys Hooke's Law σ = Eε within the elastic limit.
- Item 4 — FALSE: atoms shifting by whole lattice vectors and returning to *equivalent* (not
  original) positions is **plastic** deformation (Q2).
Items 1–3 belong to elastic; item 4 is the plastic definition. This is the [P2] pair:
| | Elastic | Plastic |
|---|---|---|
| Reversible? | yes | no |
| What moves | bonds **stretch** | atoms shift by **whole lattice vectors** |
| End position | original | equivalent (not original) |
| Law | σ = Eε | no Hooke's law |

questions.text: *Plastic* deformation is:

options.label: a
options.text: permanent; achieved by slip (dislocation glide) or twinning; atoms shift by whole lattice vectors and return to equivalent (not original) positions

questions.keyExplanation: Plastic = permanent, by slip or twinning, whole lattice-vector shifts.
questions.concise: Plastic = permanent, by slip or twinning, whole lattice-vector shifts.
questions.detailed:
**Plastic** deformation is *permanent*. It proceeds by two mechanisms — **slip**
(dislocation glide, §6.1) and **twinning** (§6.3) — and involves atoms shifting by whole lattice
vectors, ending on *equivalent* but not identical sites.
- (b) "reversible, following Hooke's law" describes *elastic* deformation.
- (c) purely elastic bond stretching describes *elastic* deformation.
- (d) it is a structural change, not a thermal effect.
**Key detail:** "equivalent, not original" — the crystal lattice is restored intact, just shifted.

questions.assertion: After plastic deformation, atoms occupy positions equivalent to — but not identical with — their original ones.
questions.reason: Slip moves each part of the crystal by whole lattice vectors (multiples of the Burgers vector), so the lattice is restored but displaced.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — equivalent but not identical positions.
questions.concise: Slip moves each part by whole lattice vectors, so the lattice is restored but displaced.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: after plastic deformation atoms occupy positions equivalent to — but not identical
  with — their originals.
- R is TRUE: slip moves each part of the crystal by **whole lattice vectors** (multiples of the
  Burgers vector), so the lattice is restored but displaced.

R correctly explains A. Because the shift is an exact lattice translation, after the slip event
every atom again finds itself in a perfect lattice site — the crystal is not left disordered.
That is why slip can produce large strains without destroying crystallinity.

questions.text: A deformed crystal contains a permanent shear offset across a crystallographic plane, with no mirror-related reorientation of one region. Which mechanism best explains the observation?

options.label: a
options.text: Twinning, in which coordinated fractional atomic shifts create a mirror-related orientation across a twin plane.

options.label: b
options.text: Elastic deformation, in which bond stretching is recovered when the applied stress is removed.

options.label: c
options.text: Grain-boundary sliding, in which adjacent grains move tangentially along their interface.

options.label: d
options.text: Slip, in which dislocations glide on a crystallographic system and leave a permanent relative shear offset.

questions.keyExplanation: The permanent offset along a defined crystallographic slip system is characteristic of slip by dislocation glide. Twinning reorients a region; elastic strain recovers; grain-boundary sliding occurs at interfaces.
questions.concise: Slip produces a permanent crystallographic shear offset through dislocation glide.
questions.detailed: Slip occurs when dislocations glide on a crystallographic plane and direction, leaving a permanent relative displacement. Twinning instead creates a mirror-related orientation through coordinated fractional shifts. Elastic deformation is reversible on unloading. Grain-boundary sliding is relative motion at a grain interface, not the crystallographic slip event described here.

questions.text: A *slip system* is one particular pair of:
questions.keyExplanation: Slip system = (slip plane, slip direction) pair.
questions.concise: A slip system = one (slip plane, slip direction) pair.
questions.detailed: A slip system is defined by a particular pair consisting of a **slip plane and a slip direction**. **(d)** is correct. Option (a), Burgers vector plus line direction, describes the geometry of a dislocation; (b) and (c) are unrelated pairs.

questions.text: The FCC slip system is:
questions.keyExplanation: FCC: {111} (4 planes) × ⟨110⟩ (3 per plane) = 12.
questions.concise: FCC: 4 {111} planes × 3 ⟨110⟩ directions per plane = 12.
questions.detailed:
```
FCC:  planes  = 4 distinct {111} close-packed planes
      dirs    = 3 ⟨110⟩ close-packed directions in each plane
      systems = 4 × 3 = 12
```
- (b) {110}⟨111⟩ = 12 is the **BCC** system (Q7).
- (c) (0001)⟨112̄0⟩ = 3 is **HCP** (Q8).
- (d) {112}⟨110⟩ = 24 is not FCC.
FCC's 12 systems all lie on close-packed planes, which is why FCC metals are so formable.

questions.text: The BCC primary slip system is:
questions.keyExplanation: BCC: {110} (6) × ⟨111⟩ (2) = 12. [P2] — do not swap with FCC.
questions.concise: BCC: 6 {110} planes × 2 ⟨111⟩ directions = 12.
questions.detailed: The primary BCC slip family is {110} planes with ⟨111⟩ directions, giving 12 systems in the conventional count used here. **(c)** is correct. Option (a) is FCC; (b) is HCP basal slip; (d) is not the primary BCC system.

questions.text: The HCP slip system is:
questions.concise: HCP: 1 basal plane × 3 ⟨112̄0⟩ directions = 3.
questions.detailed: The primary HCP slip family is basal {0001} with ⟨11̄20⟩ directions, giving three systems. **(b)** is correct. Option (a) is FCC; (c) is BCC; (d) describes a prismatic family rather than the primary basal system.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about BCC slip is/are correct?

statements.text: BCC has no truly close-packed plane; {110} is simply the most densely packed available.
At elevated temperature {112} and {123} planes also activate.
The effective total number of slip systems can approach 48.
BCC therefore behaves exactly like FCC at all temperatures.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct. Item 4 is false — this is exactly why BCC has a ductile–brittle transition and FCC does not.
questions.concise: BCC has no truly close-packed plane, activates {112}/{123} at high T, up to ~48 systems — but does *not* behave like FCC.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: BCC has no truly close-packed plane; {110} is simply the most densely packed available.
- Item 2 — TRUE: at elevated temperature {112} and {123} planes also activate.
- Item 3 — TRUE: the effective total number of slip systems can approach 48 (12 primary + others
  as temperature rises).
- Item 4 — FALSE: BCC does **not** behave like FCC at all temperatures. This is exactly why BCC
  metals (α-Fe) show a **ductile–brittle transition** while FCC metals (γ-Fe, Al, Cu) do not.
Item 4 is the false member — and it is the *opposite* of the real metallurgical significance of
the BCC structure. Note that BCC having ~12–48 systems while still being less ductile than FCC
shows that *count alone* is not sufficient; the *character* of the systems (and the lack of a
true close-packed plane) matters too.

questions.text: Which statements explain why slip commonly occurs on close-packed planes and along close-packed directions?

statements.text: Close-packed planes often provide a relatively favourable path for shear because the arrangement of atoms lowers the resistance to slip.
A short lattice translation along the slip direction gives a comparatively small Burgers vector and lowers dislocation strain energy, which scales approximately with $b^2$.
In every cubic crystal, the most densely packed plane family also has the greatest interplanar spacing.
A slip direction is energetically preferred when its Burgers-vector magnitude is as large as possible.

questions.keyExplanation: Statements 1 and 2 describe the main energetic reasons. Statement 3 is not a general geometrical rule: for a cubic crystal $d_{hkl}=a/\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2}$. Statement 4 reverses the Burgers-vector energy trend.
questions.concise: Close-packed planes favour shear, and short lattice translations reduce Burgers-vector magnitude and dislocation energy.
questions.detailed: The detailed energetic preference depends on crystal structure and dislocation character, but close-packed planes and directions commonly reduce the resistance to glide. The elastic energy per unit length scales approximately with $Gb^2$, so a smaller Burgers vector is generally favourable. The plane with the greatest planar packing density is not necessarily the plane with the greatest interplanar spacing; for cubic crystals, spacing follows $d_{hkl}=a/\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2}$. Larger $b$ raises, rather than lowers, the elastic energy.

questions.text: The von Mises criterion states that a polycrystalline aggregate needs at least how many *independent* slip systems to change shape arbitrarily without cracking at grain boundaries?
questions.keyExplanation: 5 independent slip systems (von Mises).
questions.concise: von Mises: a polycrystal needs ≥ 5 independent slip systems.
questions.detailed:
The **von Mises criterion** states that a polycrystalline aggregate needs at least
**5 independent slip systems** to change shape arbitrarily without cracking at grain boundaries.
- (a) 3 is HCP's *total* basal systems — which is why HCP fails the criterion.
- (c) 12 is FCC's/BCC's total systems.
- (d) 48 is BCC's high-temperature total.
**Why 5?** Arbitrary homogeneous shape change has 5 independent components of the strain tensor
(6 minus the volume change constraint), so you need at least 5 independent systems to satisfy
each grain's compatibility with its neighbours.

questions.assertion: HCP metals such as Zn and Mg are markedly less ductile as polycrystals than FCC metals such as Cu and Al — despite the identical 0.74 packing factor.
questions.reason: HCP's 3 basal slip systems fall well short of the 5 independent systems the von Mises criterion requires, whereas FCC has 12.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

options.label: c
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — 3 < 5, so HCP polycrystals cannot deform without cracking.
questions.concise: HCP's 3 basal systems < 5 needed, so HCP polycrystals can't deform without cracking; FCC has 12. Identical packing (0.74) does not mean identical ductility.
questions.detailed: Frenkel's sinusoidal restoring-stress model is τ = τ_max sin(2πx/b), so **(b)** is correct. Option (a) is the cosine form and is nonzero at x = 0, where the unstressed crystal should have zero restoring stress. Option (c) is only the small-displacement linear approximation; (d) is not the periodic relation.

questions.text: Use the comparison below to identify the main structural reason FCC polycrystals are usually more formable than HCP polycrystals at room temperature.

options.label: a
options.text: FCC is more formable because its ideal atomic packing factor is higher than that of HCP.

options.label: b
options.text: FCC provides more independent easy slip systems; HCP often has too few easy basal modes for compatible polycrystal deformation.

options.label: c
options.text: HCP has more accessible slip systems than FCC, so every HCP grain can accommodate arbitrary shape change.

options.label: d
options.text: The difference is explained by melting point alone; slip-system accessibility has no important role.

questions.keyExplanation: The table gives the same ideal packing factor for both structures but 12 common FCC slip systems versus only 3 easy basal HCP systems. Accessible independent deformation modes, not packing factor alone, explain the usual formability difference.
questions.concise: FCC typically offers more independent easy slip modes than HCP basal slip, despite the same ideal packing factor.
questions.detailed: Matching the small-displacement limit of the sinusoidal stress to the elastic shear stress gives τ_max ≈ Gb/(2πa). With b ≈ a, τ_max ≈ G/(2π) ≈ 0.16G, so **(d)** is correct. Options (a) and (b) are experimental-strength scales, while (c), 2πG, is not the Frenkel estimate.

questions.text: Schmid's Law is:

options.label: a
options.text: τ_R = σ sin φ sin λ

options.label: b
options.text: σ = τ_R cos φ cos λ

options.label: d
options.text: τ_R = σ cos φ cos λ

questions.keyExplanation: τ_R = σ cos φ cos λ.
questions.concise: Schmid's Law: τ_R = σ cos φ cos λ.
questions.detailed: Schmid's law is τ_R = σ cos φ cos λ. **(d)** is correct. Option (a) uses sine factors; (b) rearranges the relation incorrectly; and (c) is not Schmid's law. The angles are defined in Q15–Q16.

questions.text: In Schmid's law, φ is the angle between:

options.label: a
options.text: the tensile axis and the slip direction

options.label: b
options.text: the slip plane and the slip direction

options.label: d
options.text: the tensile (stress) axis and the slip-**plane normal**

questions.keyExplanation: φ = angle to the slip-**plane normal**. [P2]
questions.concise: φ = angle between load axis and the slip-**plane normal**.
questions.detailed: In Schmid's law, φ is the angle between the tensile axis and the slip-plane normal. **(d)** is correct. Option (a) defines λ, the angle to the slip direction; the other options do not define φ.

questions.text: For one slip system, the tensile axis makes $25^\circ$ with the slip-plane normal and $65^\circ$ with the slip direction. A student swaps the labels $\phi$ and $\lambda$ when evaluating Schmid’s law. Which statement is correct?

options.label: a
options.text: The cosine product is unchanged, but each symbol keeps its own geometric definition.

options.label: b
options.text: The result changes because Schmid’s law assigns separate cosine factors to separate directions.

options.label: c
options.text: The swap is valid only when both angles equal $45^\circ$; otherwise one factor is omitted.

options.label: d
options.text: The resolved shear stress becomes zero whenever the two angles sum to $90^\circ$.

questions.keyExplanation: The factor is $m=\cos\phi\cos\lambda$, so swapping the two cosines does not change their product. However, $\phi$ is defined relative to the slip-plane normal and $\lambda$ relative to the slip direction; their physical meanings are not interchangeable.
questions.concise: The product is symmetric in the two angles, but $\phi$ and $\lambda$ retain different geometric definitions.
questions.detailed: Schmid’s law uses $\tau_R=\sigma\cos\phi\cos\lambda$. Since multiplication is commutative, swapping the cosine factors leaves the numerical product unchanged. The angle labels nevertheless describe different geometric directions: $\phi$ is measured to the plane normal, while $\lambda$ is measured to the slip direction. The numerical coincidence does not justify redefining either angle.

questions.text: The Schmid factor m = cos φ cos λ has the range:
questions.concise: Schmid factor m = cos φ cos λ: 0 ≤ m ≤ 0.5, max at φ = λ = 45°.
questions.detailed: The Schmid factor has the range 0 ≤ m ≤ 0.5, with its maximum at φ = λ = 45°. **(c)** is correct. Option (a) ignores that the slip-plane normal and slip direction are perpendicular; (b) gives an incorrect range; (d) incorrectly makes m constant.

questions.text: A single crystal has τ_crss = 1 MPa on its most favourable slip system, oriented at φ = 45°, λ = 45°. The tensile yield stress σ_y is:
questions.keyExplanation: m = cos45°·cos45° = 0.5; σ_y = τ_crss/m = 1/0.5 = 2 MPa.
questions.concise: m = cos45°·cos45° = 0.5 → σ_y = τ_crss/m = 1/0.5 = 2 MPa.
questions.detailed: At φ = λ = 45°, m = cos45° cos45° = 0.5. Slip begins when σ_y m = τ_crss, so σ_y = 1/0.5 = 2 MPa. **(a)** is correct. Option (b) is below τ_crss even at the maximum Schmid factor; (c) assumes m = 1; and (d) belongs to the less favourable orientation in Q19.

questions.text: The *same* crystal now oriented at φ = λ = 70° has σ_y ≈:
questions.detailed: At φ = λ = 70°, m = cos²70° ≈ 0.117. Therefore σ_y = 1/0.117 ≈ 8.5 MPa, so **(b)** is correct. The other options do not satisfy σ_y = τ_crss/m.

questions.text: Comparing Q18 and Q19, changing only the orientation raised the required yield stress by roughly:
questions.keyExplanation: 8.5/2 ≈ 4× higher purely from orientation.
questions.concise: 8.5 / 2 ≈ 4× higher purely from orientation.
questions.detailed:
```
σ_y (45°) = 2 MPa
σ_y (70°) = 8.5 MPa

ratio = 8.5 / 2 ≈ 4.27 ≈ 4×
```
- (d) is the trap: the *applied* yield stress is strongly orientation-dependent even though
  τ_crss is not.
The examinable insight: **the same crystal can appear 4× weaker or stronger purely depending on
how it is loaded** — this is the origin of *crystallographic texture* effects in forming, and of
why single-crystal turbine blades are grown with a preferred orientation (Q23).

questions.text: The critical resolved shear stress τ_crss is best described as:

options.label: a
options.text: an intrinsic material property, independent of loading direction

options.label: b
options.text: a property that depends on the crystal's orientation

options.label: c
options.text: the applied tensile stress at yield

questions.keyExplanation: τ_crss is intrinsic and orientation-independent.
questions.concise: τ_crss is intrinsic — it does not depend on how the crystal is oriented.
questions.detailed:
The **critical resolved shear stress** τ_crss is the resolved shear stress that must
be reached for slip to begin on a system. It is an **intrinsic material property** — determined
by the crystal structure, bonding, temperature and purity — and is **independent of the loading
direction**.
- (b) is the trap: *σ_y* (the applied stress at yield) depends on orientation, but τ_crss does not.
- (c) is the applied stress, not the resolved critical value.
- (d) the theoretical strength is ~G/30, far higher than any real τ_crss.
This independence is precisely what makes Schmid's law powerful: measure τ_crss once in any
orientation, and you can predict σ_y in *every* orientation.

questions.text: In a tensile test, slip begins on whichever slip system has:

options.label: b
options.text: the largest Schmid factor, at the instant τ_R reaches τ_crss

questions.keyExplanation: Slip starts on the system with the largest Schmid factor.
questions.concise: Slip begins on the system with the largest Schmid factor.
questions.detailed: Each slip system experiences τ_R = σm. As the tensile stress rises, the system with the **largest Schmid factor** reaches τ_crss first. **(b)** is correct. Option (a) would require the largest applied stress; (c) and (d) are not the criterion.

questions.text: A design team compares three orientations of the same nickel-base single-crystal alloy in a matched high-temperature tensile-creep test. Use the reported results to choose the best-supported conclusion.
tableRows: Measured creep strain after the same test duration
Same alloy and γ/γ′ strengthening condition; no high-angle grain boundaries

options.label: a
options.text: [001] is preferred because it maximises the Schmid factor on every slip system and therefore encourages easy glide.

options.label: b
options.text: [001] removes the need for γ/γ′ precipitates because all single crystals are immune to creep.

options.label: c
options.text: The data show lowest creep strain near [001]; this alloy’s creep response is anisotropic, and the single crystal removes high-angle grain boundaries.

options.label: d
options.text: [001] is preferred because it makes the elastic modulus and creep response identical in every direction.

questions.keyExplanation: For the stated test data, [001] has the lowest creep strain. The result supports a favourable orientation for this alloy and test, not a universal statement that [001] maximises the Schmid factor or removes the need for precipitate strengthening.
questions.concise: The data show the lowest creep strain near [001]; crystallographic orientation matters and the single crystal avoids high-angle grain boundaries.
questions.detailed: Compare the values under identical test conditions: 0.42% for near [001] is below 0.71% for near [011] and 0.59% for near [111]. The correct inference is limited to the specified alloy and test. Nickel-base single-crystal blades retain their γ/γ′ strengthening microstructure, and eliminating high-angle grain boundaries is another major advantage. The data do not support the claim that [001] maximises resolved shear stress or makes the material isotropic.

questions.text: Slip is *impossible* (τ_R = 0) when:

options.label: b
options.text: either φ or λ equals 90° — the stress axis lies in the slip plane, or is perpendicular to the slip direction

questions.keyExplanation: τ = 0 if either angle is 90°.
questions.concise: τ = 0 if either angle = 90°.
questions.detailed: Since τ_R = σ cos φ cos λ, the resolved shear stress is zero if either φ or λ is 90°. **(b)** is correct. Option (a), φ = λ = 45°, gives the maximum Schmid factor; (c) gives a non-zero value; and (d) gives the maximum rather than zero.

questions.text: *Twinning* is:

options.label: a
options.text: dislocation glide on discrete planes producing steps of magnitude b

options.label: d
options.text: a homogeneous shear of a block of lattice into a mirror-image orientation of the parent lattice across the twin plane

questions.keyExplanation: Twinning = homogeneous shear to a mirror-image orientation.
questions.concise: Twinning = homogeneous shear producing a mirror-image orientation.
questions.detailed: Twinning is a homogeneous shear that reorients a block of lattice into a mirror-image orientation across the twin plane. **(d)** is correct. Option (a) describes slip by dislocation glide; (b) is reversible elastic bending; and (c) is grain-boundary migration.

questions.text: Match the feature to *slip* or *twinning*.
tableRows: Dislocation glide on discrete planes; sharp steps; whole multiples of b
Coordinated homogeneous shear; small fixed reorientation angle; mirrored lattice
Same lattice orientation throughout the deformed region
Reorients the deformed region into a mirror image
questions.concise: Discrete glide/steps = slip · homogeneous shear/mirror = twinning · same orientation = slip · reoriented = twin.
questions.detailed:
| Feature | Mode |
|---|---|
| Dislocation glide on discrete planes; sharp steps; whole multiples of b | **slip** |
| Coordinated homogeneous shear; small fixed reorientation angle; mirrored lattice | **twinning** |
| Same lattice orientation throughout the deformed region | **slip** |
| Reorients the deformed region into a mirror image | **twinning** |
Rows 3 and 4 are the *same* distinction expressed as a consequence — the orientation test is the
single fastest discriminator between the two modes.

questions.text: Twinning is favoured precisely where slip is difficult — namely:

statements.text: low temperature
high strain rate (impact loading)
metals with few available slip systems (HCP Zn, Mg, Ti; BCC α-Fe at low temperature)
high temperature, low strain rate in FCC metals

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 states the opposite condition.
questions.concise: Twinning is favoured where slip is difficult: low T, high strain rate, few slip systems — *not* high T/low rate in FCC.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: low temperature (thermally activated slip is suppressed).
- Item 2 — TRUE: high strain rate (impact loading gives no time for slip to operate fully).
- Item 3 — TRUE: metals with few available slip systems — HCP (Zn, Mg, Ti) and BCC α-Fe at low
  temperature.
- Item 4 — FALSE: high temperature with low strain rate is exactly the condition where **slip**
  operates easily (and where creep occurs) — twinning is *not* favoured.
Item 4 states the opposite condition. **The rule:** twinning appears where slip is *suppressed* —
cold, fast, or when slip systems are scarce.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about twinning in FCC metals is/are correct?

statements.text: FCC metals with ample slip systems (Cu, Al) rarely twin mechanically at room temperature.
Low-SFE FCC metals can still form *annealing* twins during recrystallisation.
All FCC metals twin mechanically at room temperature.
Annealing twins and mechanical twins are identical in origin.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2 correct. Item 3 is false; item 4 conflates two different origins.
questions.concise: FCC metals rarely twin mechanically at room temperature (they have plenty of slip systems), but low-SFE FCC metals do form *annealing* twins.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: FCC metals with ample slip systems (Cu, Al) rarely twin mechanically at room
  temperature.
- Item 2 — TRUE: low-SFE FCC metals can still form **annealing** twins during recrystallisation
  (the fault energy is low enough that a twin boundary is cheap).
- Item 3 — FALSE: this contradicts item 1 — *not* all FCC metals twin mechanically at RT.
- Item 4 — FALSE: annealing twins and mechanical twins have **different origins** — the former
  form during grain growth/recrystallisation (a thermally driven process), the latter under
  applied stress.
Items 3 and 4 both over-generalise. The origin distinction (annealing vs mechanical) is a good
[P2] discriminator in itself.

questions.text: Twinning matters much more for HCP than for FCC because:

statements.text: it supplies the extra deformation modes that basal slip alone cannot provide
HCP has only 3 basal slip systems
it helps HCP metals accommodate the 5 independent systems requirement
HCP has 12 slip systems

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 is false (HCP has only 3).
questions.concise: Twinning supplies the extra deformation modes HCP needs, given only 3 basal slip systems — but HCP does not have 12 systems.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: it supplies the extra deformation modes that basal slip alone cannot provide.
- Item 2 — TRUE: HCP has only 3 basal slip systems.
- Item 3 — TRUE: it helps HCP metals accommodate the 5-independent-systems requirement.
- Item 4 — FALSE: HCP has **3** primary systems, not 12 (12 belongs to FCC/BCC).
Item 4 is the transplanted number from the sibling structures — the same [P2] device as Ch. 2 Q14.
**Why this matters:** it is *why* HCP metals are more workable than a bare "3 < 5" count would
suggest — twinning provides additional, albeit limited, shape-change capability.

questions.text: The shape change produced by twinning is:

options.label: a
options.text: step-like, in whole multiples of b

options.label: d
options.text: homogeneous shear producing a small fixed angle of reorientation

questions.keyExplanation: Homogeneous shear, small fixed angle — contrast with slip's whole-multiple steps.
questions.concise: Twinning: homogeneous shear, small fixed reorientation angle.
questions.detailed: Twinning produces a homogeneous shear and a small, fixed crystallographic reorientation. **(d)** is correct. Option (a), step-like displacement in whole multiples of b, describes slip; (b) and (c) incorrectly deny permanent plastic shape change.

questions.assertion: Mechanical twinning is common in BCC metals at low temperature or high strain rate.
questions.reason: These are exactly the conditions under which slip is restricted, so the alternative shear mechanism becomes favourable.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — twinning activates where slip is restricted.
questions.concise: Low T / high strain rate restrict slip, so twinning becomes favourable.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: mechanical twinning is common in BCC metals at low temperature or high strain rate.
- R is TRUE: these are exactly the conditions under which slip is restricted, so the alternative
  shear mechanism (twinning) becomes favourable.

R correctly explains A. This is Q27 applied specifically to BCC α-Fe — twinning is a *backup*
mechanism that switches on when the primary mechanism (slip) is starved of thermal activation
or time.

questions.text: Which material condition is most likely to show a sharp upper yield point followed by a stress drop and a lower-yield plateau?

options.label: a
options.text: A low-carbon ferritic steel in which mobile carbon or nitrogen atoms pin dislocations before yield.

options.label: b
options.text: A high-purity annealed copper with few interstitial solutes and continuous yielding.

options.label: c
options.text: A precipitation-hardened aluminium alloy whose strength is controlled mainly by cutting or bypassing precipitates.

options.label: d
options.text: A heavily cold-worked FCC alloy whose flow stress rises through dislocation interactions.

questions.keyExplanation: Mobile interstitial C/N atoms can form atmospheres around dislocations in ferritic steel. A higher stress is needed to unpin them; once dislocations break away, deformation continues at a lower stress.
questions.concise: The classical yield-point phenomenon is associated with interstitial-solute pinning and breakaway in ferritic steels.
questions.detailed: A Cottrell atmosphere pins dislocations in ferritic steel. Initial motion requires a higher upper-yield stress; once dislocations break free, additional dislocations can move and the stress drops to the lower-yield region. Precipitation strengthening and work hardening change flow stress by different mechanisms and do not, by themselves, identify this characteristic upper/lower yield sequence.

questions.text: After ageing ferritic steel, dislocations require a larger stress to begin moving. Which microstructural feature is the defining Cottrell-atmosphere mechanism?

options.label: a
options.text: A vacancy cluster around the line that changes the Burgers vector and removes the elastic strain field.

options.label: b
options.text: A coherent precipitate in the matrix that strengthens the alloy through cutting or bypassing.

options.label: c
options.text: Interstitial C/N atoms collect in an edge dislocation’s tensile field and pin its glide.

options.label: d
options.text: A solute-enriched grain-boundary region that chiefly pins boundary migration rather than a dislocation.

questions.keyExplanation: Interstitial carbon or nitrogen segregates to the tensile region below an edge dislocation's extra half-plane, forming a Cottrell atmosphere that pins dislocation motion until sufficient stress unpins it.
questions.concise: Cottrell atmospheres are interstitial C/N clusters in the tensile field of a dislocation that pin its motion.
questions.detailed: The tensile field below an edge dislocation attracts interstitial carbon and nitrogen. Their segregation lowers local elastic energy and creates a Cottrell atmosphere. A higher stress is needed to break the dislocation free. Vacancy clusters, precipitate obstacles and solute-decorated grain boundaries are distinct defect/strengthening mechanisms.

questions.text: Oversized interstitial atoms such as carbon preferentially segregate to which region around an edge dislocation, and why?

options.label: a
options.text: The compressive region above the extra half-plane, because oversized atoms fit best where the lattice is already crowded.

options.label: b
options.text: The shear region on the slip plane, because the solute lowers the resolved shear stress by changing the slip direction.

options.label: c
options.text: The far-field neutral region, where the dislocation's stress field vanishes and solute atoms experience the strongest attraction.

options.label: d
options.text: The tensile region below the extra half-plane, where local expansion reduces the elastic misfit of an oversized interstitial.

questions.keyExplanation: An oversized interstitial causes local compression of its own; it preferentially occupies an existing tensile region below the extra half-plane, reducing the combined elastic strain energy.
questions.concise: Oversized interstitials favour the tensile zone below an edge dislocation's extra half-plane.
questions.detailed: An oversized interstitial generates a local compressive misfit. It lowers total elastic energy by segregating to the tensile field below the extra half-plane. The compressed region has the wrong sign for this size misfit; the shear field is not the primary hydrostatic interaction, and the far field has little stress to attract the solute.

questions.text: The extra stress (the upper yield point) is needed to:

options.label: d
options.text: tear a dislocation free from its Cottrell atmosphere, or to nucleate fresh unpinned dislocations

questions.keyExplanation: Freeing a pinned dislocation, or nucleating fresh ones.
questions.concise: The upper yield point is the extra stress to free a pinned dislocation.
questions.detailed: The upper yield point is the extra stress needed to free dislocations pinned by Cottrell atmospheres or to activate fresh unpinned sources. **(d)** is correct. Options (a)–(c) do not describe the unlocking process.

questions.text: The *Lüders band* is:

options.label: a
options.text: a visible deformation front that sweeps along the gauge length at the lower yield stress, until the whole gauge length has yielded

questions.keyExplanation: Lüders band = propagating deformation front at the lower yield stress.
questions.concise: Lüders band = propagating deformation front at the lower yield stress.
questions.detailed:
A **Lüders band** is a visible deformation front that sweeps along the gauge length
at the **lower** yield stress. Yielding proceeds *inhomogeneously*: the band nucleates, then
propagates, until the entire gauge length has yielded — only then does uniform strain hardening
begin.
- (b), (c), (d) are unrelated phenomena.
The practical significance: Lüders strains produce an undesirable surface roughness ("stretcher
strains") on formed mild-steel sheet, which is why the phenomenon matters industrially — and why
steel is often temper-rolled (skin-passed) to eliminate it.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about *strain ageing* is/are correct?

statements.text: A specimen strained just past the yield point, unloaded, and left (or gently warmed) allows solute to diffuse back to stationary dislocations and re-form Cottrell atmospheres.
On reloading, the yield-point phenomenon reappears — often at a *higher* stress than the original upper yield point.
Ageing increases strength and hardness but reduces ductility and toughness.
Strain ageing eliminates the yield-point phenomenon permanently.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct. Item 4 is false — ageing *restores* the yield point. [P1]
questions.concise: After a rest, solute re-pin the dislocations → yield point returns at higher stress; strength up, ductility down — ageing does *not* eliminate the yield point permanently.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: a specimen strained just past the yield point, unloaded, and left (or gently
  warmed) allows solute to diffuse back to stationary dislocations and re-form Cottrell atmospheres.
- Item 2 — TRUE: on reloading, the yield-point phenomenon reappears — often at a *higher* stress
  than the original upper yield point.
- Item 3 — TRUE: ageing increases strength and hardness but reduces ductility and toughness.
- Item 4 — FALSE: strain ageing **restores** (re-establishes) the yield-point phenomenon; it does
  not eliminate it. Item 4 states the exact opposite.
**The complete cycle to memorise:**
```
1. Yield → dislocations break free of atmospheres → continuous flow
2. Unload → dislocations stationary
3. Rest / warm → solute diffuses back → atmospheres re-form
4. Reload → yield point REAPPEARS, at a HIGHER stress
5. Consequence: ↑ strength & hardness, ↓ ductility & toughness
```

questions.text: *Blue brittleness* is:

options.label: a
options.text: a drop in impact toughness in steel when forming is done at roughly 200–300 °C — the same range that develops a blue temper-colour oxide film, and in which accelerated strain ageing peaks

options.label: b
options.text: a colour-plate defect on stainless steel

questions.keyExplanation: Blue brittleness ≈ 200–300 °C, coinciding with blue oxide film and peak strain ageing.
questions.concise: Blue brittleness ≈ 200–300 °C: accelerated strain ageing + blue oxide film + drop in impact toughness.
questions.detailed:
**Blue brittleness** is a drop in impact toughness when steel is formed at roughly
**200–300 °C**. Three things coincide in that range:
1. strain ageing is *thermally accelerated* (C and N diffuse faster → rapid re-pinning),
2. the steel develops a **blue** temper-colour oxide film,
3. impact toughness falls.
- (b) a colour-plate defect is a surface-finish issue, not a mechanical property.
- (c) it is a *loss* of toughness, not a toughening treatment.
- (d) it is not a coating.
**[P2] the name's trap:** "blue" refers to the *colour of the oxide film* in that temperature
range, not to the mechanism. The mechanism is accelerated strain ageing — the same phenomenon as
Q37, just sped up by heat.

questions.text: A copper single crystal has a critical resolved shear stress of 1.0 MPa on its most favourably oriented slip system and is loaded such that φ = 30° and λ = 60°. The applied tensile stress at which it yields is closest to:
questions.detailed: The Schmid factor is m = cos30° cos60° = 0.8660 × 0.5 = 0.433. Thus σ_y = τ_crss/m = 1.0/0.433 ≈ 2.31 MPa, so **(c)** is correct. Option (a) uses only one cosine; (b) overestimates the required stress; and (d) does not apply the division by m.

questions.text: The jerky, serrated flow known as the Portevin–Le Chatelier effect, seen during a constant-rate tensile test, is caused by:

options.label: a
options.text: dynamic strain ageing — solute atoms repeatedly re-pin moving dislocations, which then break away again

options.label: b
options.text: periodic fracture of brittle inclusions ahead of the plastic front

options.label: c
options.text: intermittent adiabatic heating that softens the specimen

options.label: d
options.text: stick–slip of the specimen in the grips

questions.keyExplanation: Serrated flow is dynamic strain ageing — moving dislocations are repeatedly re-pinned and then break away.
questions.concise: Serrated flow = Portevin–Le Chatelier = dynamic strain ageing operating during the test.
questions.detailed: The Portevin–Le Chatelier effect is dynamic strain ageing: diffusing solute atoms repeatedly pin moving dislocations, which then break away as the applied stress rises. This repeated pinning and release produces serrated flow. **(a)** is correct; the other options are not the mechanism.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about cross-slip is/are correct?

statements.text: A screw dislocation has its Burgers vector parallel to its line, so it can glide on any plane containing b.
Low stacking-fault energy makes cross-slip difficult and promotes coarse planar slip bands.
Cross-slip allows a gliding dislocation to bypass obstacles such as precipitates and pile-ups.
Edge dislocations cross-slip readily because their glide plane is not fixed.

questions.keyExplanation: Cross-slip is a screw-dislocation property, low SFE keeps slip planar and cross-slip bypasses obstacles — edge dislocations have a fixed glide plane.
questions.concise: Cross-slip is a screw-dislocation property; low SFE keeps slip planar; edge dislocations cannot cross-slip because their glide plane is fixed.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: for a screw dislocation b ∥ line, so no unique glide plane exists and it can move on any plane containing b.
- Item 2 — TRUE: a widely dissociated partial pair (low SFE) must constrict before changing planes, so slip stays planar and coarse bands form.
- Item 3 — TRUE: sidestepping obstacles is how plastic flow continues past precipitates and pile-ups.
- Item 4 — FALSE: an edge dislocation has b ⊥ line, so b and the line define one and only one glide plane.

questions.assertion: A single crystal of zinc can be extended to large strains in tension even though it possesses only three primary slip systems.
questions.reason: The requirement for five independent slip systems applies only where grains are mutually constrained, as in a polycrystal.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: The five-independent-systems rule constrains only mutually bounded grains, so a free single crystal can deform on three systems.
questions.concise: The five-independent-systems requirement is a grain-constraint condition, so a free single crystal deforms on far fewer systems.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: a Zn single crystal of favourable orientation extends substantially using basal slip plus twinning.
- R is TRUE: von Mises' five independent systems are demanded only when each grain must change shape in compatibility with its neighbours.
- With no neighbours to satisfy, a single crystal needs just enough systems for the imposed shape change, so three can suffice.
R correctly explains A — this is the precise qualification to the von Mises criterion: it constrains *polycrystals*, which is why HCP single crystals work while HCP aggregates crack.

questions.text: A crystal is pulled in tension at an orientation φ = λ = 60° and yields at an applied stress of 400 MPa. Its critical resolved shear stress is:
questions.keyExplanation: m = cos²60° = 0.25, hence τ_crss = σ_y × m = 400 × 0.25 = 100 MPa.
questions.detailed: With φ = λ = 60°, m = cos²60° = 0.25. Therefore τ_crss = σ_y m = 400 × 0.25 = 100 MPa, so **(b)** is correct. Options (a), (c), and (d) use incorrect Schmid factors.

questions.text: In HCP metals the dominant slip system is governed mainly by the c/a ratio. Which statement is correct?

options.label: a
options.text: All HCP metals slip on the basal plane whatever the c/a ratio, because it is always the most densely packed

options.label: b
options.text: Metals with c/a < 1.633 (Ti, Zr) favour prismatic {101̄0}⟨112̄0⟩ slip, while those with c/a > 1.633 (Zn, Cd) retain basal slip

options.label: c
options.text: c/a has no effect, since every HCP metal has the same atomic packing factor of 0.74

options.label: d
options.text: Metals with c/a > 1.633 (Zn, Cd) favour pyramidal ⟨a⟩ slip exclusively

questions.keyExplanation: Below the ideal c/a = 1.633 (Ti, Zr) prismatic slip dominates, above it (Zn, Cd) basal slip is retained.
questions.concise: c/a < 1.633 → prism slip (Ti, Zr); c/a > 1.633 → basal slip retained (Zn, Cd).
questions.detailed: The c/a ratio changes which HCP plane family is most densely packed. Ti and Zr, with c/a below the ideal value, favour prismatic ⟨a⟩ slip; Zn and Cd, with c/a above the ideal value, retain basal slip. **(b)** is correct. Option (a) incorrectly makes basal slip universal; (c) confuses packing factor with plane density; (d) incorrectly claims exclusive pyramidal slip.

questions.text: A zinc single crystal is pulled at σ = 100 MPa with φ = 45° and λ = 60°. The resolved shear stress acting on that slip system is:
questions.detailed: τ_R = σ cos φ cos λ = 100 × cos45° × cos60° = 100 × 0.7071 × 0.5 ≈ 35.4 MPa. **(b)** is correct. The other options apply only one projection or use the wrong angle.

questions.text: Match each term with its correct description.
tableRows: (a) a deformation front that propagates at the lower yield stress
(b) the stress at which a pinned dislocation is first torn free
(c) diffusion of solute to stationary dislocations after unloading, restoring the yield point
(d) repeated pinning and breakaway of moving dislocations, giving serrated flow
questions.keyExplanation: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b: ageing is re-pinning after rest, PLC is pinning during flow, the band is the front, the upper point is the breakaway stress.
questions.concise: Ageing = re-pinning after a rest; PLC = pinning during flow; Lüders band = propagating front; upper yield point = breakaway stress.
questions.detailed:
| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| Strain ageing | solute diffuses to *stationary* dislocations after unloading, yield point returns |
| Portevin–Le Chatelier | pinning and breakaway *during* straining, giving serrated flow |
| Lüders band | the deformation front travelling at the lower yield stress |
| Upper yield point | the stress needed to free the first pinned dislocation |
The natural pairing: two *mechanisms* (static ageing, dynamic ageing) and two *consequences* (a stress value, a deformation front). (a) shuffles all four; (b) and (d) swap matched pairs.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about the deformation of HCP metals is/are correct?

statements.text: Basal slip alone cannot produce any strain component along the c-axis.
{101̄2} extension twins supply the c-axis extension that basal slip cannot provide in Zn and Mg.
Prismatic and pyramidal slip become more active at elevated temperature, which improves workability.
At room temperature HCP metals are more ductile than FCC metals, thanks to twinning.

questions.keyExplanation: Items 1–3 are correct; item 4 reverses the truth — HCP polycrystals are markedly less ductile than FCC ones.
questions.concise: Basal slip cannot strain the c-axis, extension twins supply it, non-basal slip activates on heating — but HCP metals stay *less* ductile than FCC.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: every basal shear lies in the basal plane, so no strain component along c can be produced.
- Item 2 — TRUE: {101̄2} extension twins are the standard source of c-axis extension in Zn and Mg.
- Item 3 — TRUE: prism and pyramidal slip are thermally activated and dominate the hot-working range.
- Item 4 — FALSE: it reverses the established fact — HCP polycrystals are markedly *less* ductile than FCC (Q12), because three basal systems plus twinning still fall short of the von Mises five.
Each HCP mode covers what the others cannot: basal (in-plane), twins (c-axis), non-basal slip (high temperature).

questions.text: The Portevin–Le Chatelier effect is a *dynamic* strain-ageing phenomenon: re-pinning occurs while the specimen is actively deforming, unlike static strain ageing, which acts on dislocations that are at rest after unloading.
questions.keyExplanation: True — the Portevin–Le Chatelier effect is re-pinning during ongoing straining, whereas static ageing acts on dislocations at rest.
questions.concise: PLC is dynamic ageing — re-pinning races against ongoing straining; static ageing acts on dislocations at rest.
questions.detailed:
**True.** The two phenomena differ only in *when* the dislocations are stationary:
- **Static ageing** — specimen unloaded, dislocations at rest, solute diffuses in over minutes or hours (faster if warmed) and the yield point returns.
- **Dynamic ageing (PLC)** — dislocations are moving under load, yet solute still catches them intermittently, so pinning and breakaway alternate and the trace serrates.
- Raise the strain rate or lower the temperature far enough and the serrations disappear, because diffusion can no longer keep up.

questions.text: Stage II (linear hardening) of the single-crystal tensile stress–strain curve is best described as:

options.label: a
options.text: a regime of high, nearly constant hardening rate arising from rapid multiplication and the build-up of dislocation tangles and pile-ups on intersecting systems

options.label: b
options.text: an easy-glide region in which one slip system operates alone at a low hardening rate

options.label: c
options.text: a parabolic region in which dynamic recovery by cross-slip offsets further hardening

options.label: d
options.text: a plateau of zero hardening followed by necking

questions.keyExplanation: Stage II is the high, nearly constant hardening-rate region produced by tangles and pile-ups on intersecting systems.
questions.concise: Stage II = high, nearly constant hardening rate from tangles and pile-ups on intersecting systems.
questions.detailed: Stage II is the high, nearly constant work-hardening-rate region caused by dislocation multiplication and the formation of tangles and pile-ups on intersecting slip systems. **(a)** is correct. Option (b) describes Stage I easy glide; (c) describes Stage III with dynamic recovery; (d) is not the Stage II response.

questions.text: A single crystal with τ_crss = 1.0 MPa yields at σ_y = 4.0 MPa when oriented symmetrically (φ = λ = θ). The angle θ is:
questions.keyExplanation: m = τ_crss/σ_y = 1/4 = 0.25 = cos²θ, so cos θ = 0.5 and θ = 60°.
questions.concise: m = τ_crss/σ_y = 1/4 = 0.25 = cos²θ, so cos θ = 0.5 and θ = 60°.
questions.detailed:
```
m = τ_crss / σ_y = 1.0 / 4.0 = 0.25
m = cos²θ  →  cos θ = √0.25 = 0.50  →  θ = 60°
```
- (a) 45° gives m = 0.50 and would predict σ_y = 2 MPa; (b) 50° gives m ≈ 0.41, σ_y ≈ 2.42 MPa; (d) 70° gives m ≈ 0.117, σ_y ≈ 8.5 MPa.
- Note θ = 45° is the *minimum* symmetric angle — any smaller would violate φ + λ ≥ 90°.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about strain ageing in steel is/are correct?

statements.text: Bake-hardened automotive sheet gains yield strength because the paint-bake cycle (about 170 °C) lets carbon re-pin the dislocations introduced during forming.
Serrated flow in a tensile test at intermediate temperature is caused by dynamic strain ageing — the Portevin–Le Chatelier effect.
Holding the steel at a temperature too low for carbon diffusion prevents ageing, so no yield point is restored on reloading.
Strain ageing lowers the yield strength and raises ductility and toughness.

questions.keyExplanation: Items 1–3 are correct; item 4 reverses the effect — ageing raises strength and hardness and lowers ductility and toughness.
questions.concise: Bake hardening and PLC are both ageing effects, no diffusion means no ageing, and item 4 reverses the true property changes.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: bake-hardened sheet is formed, then paint-baked near 170 °C; interstitial C re-pins the forming dislocations and yield strength rises by tens of MPa.
- Item 2 — TRUE: serrated flow is dynamic strain ageing, the Portevin–Le Chatelier effect.
- Item 3 — TRUE: ageing *requires* diffusion; too cold for C to move and no atmospheres re-form, so yielding stays continuous.
- Item 4 — FALSE: ageing raises strength and hardness and *reduces* ductility and toughness — the exact opposite.
Bake hardening is the industrial *use* of a mechanism that is otherwise a nuisance (Q37, Q40).

questions.text: The springback of a steel sheet after bending in a press brake is due to:

options.label: a
options.text: strain ageing that occurs while the punch retracts

options.label: b
options.text: thermal contraction of the sheet and the die

options.label: d
options.text: elastic recovery on unloading — the elastic part of the strain is recovered while the plastic part remains

questions.keyExplanation: Springback is elastic recovery: the elastic strain is reversed on unloading while the plastic strain is permanent.
questions.concise: Springback = elastic recovery on unloading; the plastic strain stays behind.
questions.detailed: Springback is elastic recovery on unloading: the elastic part of the bending strain is recovered while the plastic part remains. **(d)** is correct. Strain ageing, thermal contraction and recrystallisation are not the cause of ordinary press-brake springback.

questions.assertion: Mild-steel sheet that has not been skin-passed develops visible surface markings — stretcher strains — when it is formed.
questions.reason: Temper-rolling is carried out to introduce fresh Cottrell atmospheres and reinstate the sharp upper yield point.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: A is true; R is false because temper-rolling destroys the sharp yield point by pre-deforming the sheet, it does not reinstate it.
questions.concise: Un-skin-passed sheet does show stretcher strains, but temper-rolling *removes* the yield point instead of reinstating it.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: an un-skin-passed sheet can retain a sharp yield point and form Lüders markings during subsequent forming.
- R is FALSE: temper-rolling pre-deforms the sheet and removes the sharp yield-point behaviour; it does not reinstate it.
Therefore A is true and R is false: **(d)** is correct.

questions.text: Four specimens of the same metal, each with τ_crss = 1.0 MPa, are oriented as follows: P — φ = 45°, λ = 45°; Q — φ = 55°, λ = 70°; R — φ = 75°, λ = 75°; S — φ = 50°, λ = 80°. Which specimen requires the highest applied tensile stress to yield?
questions.keyExplanation: Specimen R has the smallest Schmid factor, m = cos²75° ≈ 0.067, and so needs the largest stress, σ_y ≈ 14.9 MPa.
questions.concise: R has the smallest Schmid factor, m = cos²75° ≈ 0.067, so it needs the largest stress, σ_y ≈ 14.9 MPa.
questions.detailed: For each specimen, σ_y = τ_crss/m. The Schmid factors are P = 0.500, Q ≈ 0.196, R ≈ 0.067 and S ≈ 0.112. Specimen R has the smallest m and therefore requires the highest applied stress. **(c)** is correct.

questions.text: At the atomic level, twinning differs from slip in that during twinning:

options.label: a
options.text: only alternate atomic planes move, each by a whole lattice vector

options.label: b
options.text: each successive atomic plane shifts by a fraction of an atomic spacing, so the shear accumulates uniformly through the twinned volume

options.label: c
options.text: all of the shear is concentrated on one glide plane

options.label: d
options.text: atoms are displaced to interstitial sites, leaving a planar vacancy sheet

questions.keyExplanation: Every atomic plane moves by a fraction of a spacing, accumulating to the fixed total twin shear, unlike slip's whole-b steps.
questions.concise: Twinning moves every plane by a fraction of a spacing, accumulating to fixed total shear — not whole-b steps on one plane.
questions.detailed:
- The hallmark of twinning: plane *n* shifts by n/N of an atomic spacing relative to plane 1, so the displacement grows linearly and the whole volume shears uniformly into the mirror orientation.
- (a) and (c) describe slip — whole lattice vectors, concentrated on a few discrete glide planes; (d) describes a planar defect, not a shear mechanism.
- The fixed total shear (set by twin geometry, not by applied stress) is why the twin shape cannot be varied, unlike slip, which can be arbitrarily large.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about the deformation textures produced by working is/are correct?

statements.text: Heavily rolled FCC metals develop rolling textures such as the brass type {110}⟨112⟩ and the copper type {112}⟨110⟩.
Wire-drawn FCC metals develop a ⟨110⟩ fibre texture with ⟨110⟩ parallel to the wire axis.
Drawn BCC wire develops a strong ⟨111⟩ fibre texture, with ⟨100⟩ as a secondary component.
Recrystallisation annealing simply leaves the deformation texture unchanged.

questions.keyExplanation: Items 1–3 are correct; item 4 is false because annealing replaces the deformation texture with a recrystallisation texture.
questions.concise: Rolling gives brass/copper textures, FCC wire a ⟨110⟩ fibre, BCC wire ⟨111⟩ — annealing replaces, not preserves, the deformation texture.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: rolled FCC sheets develop the brass type {110}⟨112⟩ and copper type {112}⟨110⟩ rolling textures.
- Item 2 — TRUE: drawing aligns ⟨110⟩ along the wire axis, giving a ⟨110⟩ fibre texture.
- Item 3 — TRUE: drawn BCC wire is strongly ⟨111⟩ with ⟨100⟩ secondary.
- Item 4 — FALSE: recrystallisation nucleates new grains with preferred orientations, *replacing* the deformation texture with an annealing texture (which is why box annealing is chosen to give soft, formable sheet).
These textures are why properties differ between the rolling, transverse and through-thickness directions — crystallographic anisotropy, the bulk legacy of Q20's single-crystal orientation effect.

questions.text: Cooling α-iron from room temperature to −196 °C raises its yield stress far more than it raises that of aluminium. The best explanation is:

options.label: a
options.text: aluminium has a much higher melting point than α-iron

options.label: b
options.text: both metals have twelve slip systems, so their temperature dependence must be identical

options.label: c
options.text: BCC slip is thermally activated on a non-close-packed plane, so τ_crss climbs steeply when thermal assistance is removed, whereas FCC slip on close-packed {111} planes is only weakly temperature-dependent

options.label: d
options.text: cooling creates additional slip systems in the BCC lattice

questions.keyExplanation: BCC slip needs thermal activation on a non-close-packed plane, so its τ_crss is far more temperature-sensitive than FCC's.
questions.concise: BCC slip lacks a close-packed plane and is thermally activated, so its τ_crss is far more temperature-sensitive than FCC's.
questions.detailed: BCC iron has a relatively high Peierls barrier on non-close-packed slip planes, so glide is strongly thermally activated and its yield stress rises sharply on cooling. FCC aluminium has close-packed {111} slip with a much lower, less temperature-sensitive barrier. **(c)** is correct. Options (a), (b), and (d) do not explain the contrasting temperature dependence.

questions.text: Two slip systems in the same crystal, each with τ_crss = 0.6 MPa, have Schmid factors of 0.45 and 0.30. The tensile stresses at which they reach τ_crss are, respectively:
questions.keyExplanation: σ = τ_crss/m gives 0.6/0.45 = 1.33 MPa for the first system and 0.6/0.30 = 2.00 MPa for the second.
questions.concise: σ = τ_crss/m gives 0.6/0.45 = 1.33 MPa and 0.6/0.30 = 2.00 MPa.
questions.detailed: The required tensile stress is σ = τ_crss/m. For m₁ = 0.45, σ₁ = 0.6/0.45 = 1.33 MPa; for m₂ = 0.30, σ₂ = 0.6/0.30 = 2.00 MPa. **(a)** is correct. The larger Schmid factor reaches the critical resolved shear stress at the lower applied tensile stress.
